\begin{comment}
OLD VERSION
\paragraph{Update cost evaluation.}
We study whether normalization improves graph updates by avoiding attribute
replication induced by functional dependencies. In the normalized schema, each
attribute value is stored only once per key. By contrast, folding $X\rightarrow Y$
copies the attributes of $Y$ except its key into each referencing $X$, so every copy
must be updated. We consider eight TPC-H foreign key edges: $L\rightarrow PS$
($e_1$), $L\rightarrow O$ ($e_2$), $PS\rightarrow P$ ($e_3$),
$PS\rightarrow S$ ($e_4$), $O\rightarrow C$ ($e_5$), $C\rightarrow N$
($e_6$), $S\rightarrow N$ ($e_7$), and $N\rightarrow R$ ($e_8$). Their
subsets define $2^8=256$ schema variants. For each variant, selected relationships are folded, while the others are inherited by the resulting nodes. If a relation involved in a fold is still referenced by another relationship, its original node is retained. This ensures that the resulting schema is independent of fold order. We apply the same updates to the normalized
and folded schemas to isolate the effect of data duplication on update cost from
differences in the number of references to each key.
The normalized baseline and each folded variant use identical update cases and
corresponding key indexes. Only the terminal relation of each fold path is
updated, with all folded copies modified together. For update case $i$, $U_{D,i}$
and $U_{N,i}$ denote the update times in the folded and normalized schemas.
We report the minimum, median, and maximum of $U_D$ and compute
$\Delta_U=\operatorname{median}_i(U_{D,i}-U_{N,i})$. A positive
$\Delta_U$ indicates an advantage for normalization. We evaluate all variants
but report one representative for each distinct combination of a terminal relation
and the folds that cause its redundancy. All differences are computed as the folded schema minus the normalized schema. $\Delta N$, $\Delta E$, and $\Delta C$ denote changes in the numbers of graph nodes, graph edges, and property cells, respectively. We also measure the one-time normalization cost of
rebuilding participating nodes, relationships, and indexes from folded data.

\end{comment}


\section{Experiments Evaluation} \label{sec:experiments}

Our evaluation asks two questions. First, how much does normalization reduce
update latency by eliminating replicated attributes (RQ1)? Second, how much query
time can de-normalization save, and is this saving commensurate with the cost
of constructing the corresponding de-normalized schema (RQ2)? We study both effects
on the same TPC-H graph and report the schema transformation costs separately.

\subsection{Experimental Setup}

\paragraph{System and protocol.}
We run all experiments on a MacBook Pro running macOS~26.6, equipped with an
Apple M5 processor with 10 CPU cores and 16~GB of memory. We use
Neo4j~2026.06.0 on OpenJDK~21 and the Neo4j Python driver~6.2.0. Each
comparison between normalized and de-normalized designs uses the same 50
update cases or query parameter bindings. We measure wall-clock time at the
client, including transaction commit for updates and complete result
consumption for queries. One-time construction and normalization costs are
measured separately.

\paragraph{Schema and dataset.}
We use TPC-H at SF = 0.1, with each of its eight relations represented by a
node label: \textsf{LINEITEM} ($L$), \textsf{PARTSUPP} ($PS$),
\textsf{PART} ($P$), \textsf{ORDERS} ($O$), \textsf{CUSTOMER} ($C$),
\textsf{SUPPLIER} ($S$), \textsf{NATION} ($N$), and \textsf{REGION} ($R$).
Each tuple is represented as a node, each column value as a property, and each
foreign-key reference as a directed relationship. The normalized graph contains
866,602 nodes, 1,527,169 relationships, and 11,666,267 non-null property cells.
Neo4j Node Key constraints enforce the primary keys, with \textsf{LINEITEM} and
\textsf{PARTSUPP} retaining their composite keys.

\subsection{Update Cost Evaluation}
We study whether normalization improves graph updates by avoiding attribute
replication induced by functional dependencies. In the normalized schema, each
attribute value is stored only once per key. By contrast, denormalizing along
$X\rightarrow Y$ copies the attributes of $Y$ except its key into each
referencing $X$, so every copy must be updated. We consider eight TPC-H foreign
key edges: $L\rightarrow PS$
($e_1$), $L\rightarrow O$ ($e_2$), $PS\rightarrow P$ ($e_3$),
$PS\rightarrow S$ ($e_4$), $O\rightarrow C$ ($e_5$), $C\rightarrow N$
($e_6$), $S\rightarrow N$ ($e_7$), and $N\rightarrow R$ ($e_8$). Their
subsets define $2^8=256$ schema variants. For each variant, attributes are
copied along the selected relationships, while the remaining relationships are
inherited by the resulting nodes. If a relation involved in denormalization is
still referenced by another relationship, its original node is retained. This
ensures that the resulting
schema is independent of processing order. We apply the same updates to the
normalized and denormalized schemas to isolate the effect of data duplication
on update cost from differences in the number of references to each key. The
normalized baseline and each denormalized variant use identical update cases
and corresponding key indexes. Only the terminal relation of each
denormalization path is updated, with all copies modified together. For update
case $i$, $U_{D,i}$ and $U_{N,i}$ denote the update times in the denormalized
and normalized schemas.
We report the minimum, median, and maximum of $U_D$ and compute
$\Delta_U=\operatorname{median}_i(U_{D,i}-U_{N,i})$. A positive
$\Delta_U$ indicates an advantage for normalization. We evaluate all variants
but report one representative for each distinct combination of a terminal
relation and the relationships that cause its redundancy. All differences are
computed as the denormalized schema minus the normalized schema. $\Delta N$,
$\Delta E$, and $\Delta C$ denote changes in the numbers of graph nodes, graph
edges, and property cells, respectively. We also measure the one-time
normalization cost of rebuilding participating nodes, relationships, and indexes
from denormalized data.

At SF = 0.1, Table~\ref{tab:denorm_update_results} shows that normalized update
latency remains stable between 5.0 and 6.0~ms across the evaluated relations, while
denormalized update latency generally increases as attribute replication accumulates
along longer paths. Normalization reduces update time in 36 of the 39 reported cases.
The three exceptions are $e_1$ ($L\rightarrow PS$), $e_2$ ($L\rightarrow O$),
and $e_8$ ($N\rightarrow R$), whose differences are approximately 1.0~ms or
less. The largest benefit occurs for REGION
with $\{e_1,e_2,e_4,e_5,e_6,e_7,e_8\}$. This schema contains 18.54M additional property
cells, and its median update latency increases from 6.0 to 995.4~ms, resulting in
a 989.4~ms saving from normalization. As data replication increases, the time required
for normalization generally increases, from 0.3 to 65.7~s across the evaluated schemas.


\subsubsection{Case Study}
To illustrate how data replication affects an individual update, we examine a
REGION update at SF = 0.1. We apply the same REGION update to the normalized
schema and to 16 representative denormalized schemas. We select paired update
group 8 from the 50 REGION cases. These schemas cover all distinct
denormalization choices along
the paths $L\rightarrow O\rightarrow C\rightarrow N\rightarrow R$ and
$L\rightarrow PS\rightarrow S\rightarrow N\rightarrow R$. In all cases, we
update \texttt{r\_comment} for \texttt{r\_regionkey}=2. Each reported update
time is the median of ten repetitions, while the number of stored copies and
additional property cells varies across schemas.

\begin{figure}[htbp]

    \includegraphics[width=0.47\textwidth]{figures/case_study_delta_vs_copies.png}

Table~\ref{tab:region_case_study} reports the measurements for paired update
group 8, while Fig.~\ref{fig:trade_off_schema} relates the two costs to REGION
copies on the horizontal axis and $\Delta C$ through color. The normalized
update remains at 6.0~ms because each REGION value is stored once. Across
configurations containing 5 to 255.1K copies, denormalized update latency
generally increases from 5.0~ms to 0.91~s. The two shallowest configurations
yield differences of $-1.0$ and $-0.1$~ms; the remaining 14 configurations save
7.0 to 904.1~ms through normalization. Copy count alone, however, does not
explain all variation. At comparable copy counts of 137.4K and 138.7K,
configurations with 8.08M and 11.41M additional cells save 397.9 and 428.8~ms,
respectively. Normalization time also generally increases from 0.32 to
65.74~s. Overall, higher replication multiplicity and larger schemas are
associated with higher update cost.





\subsubsection{Scale Factor Influence}
To isolate the influence of data scale, we repeat the TPC-H experiment at
SF = 0.01 and SF = 0.1. We focus on NATION and REGION because they provide
15 and 16 representative de-normalization edge sets, respectively; the other
evaluated terminal relations have only one or two strategies and therefore do not
show an overall trend.
Increasing SF by a factor of ten enlarges the
fact and scale-dependent relations while preserving the schema design.
Consequently, strategies whose de-normalization paths reach these relations
create more copies of each terminal-relation value. For each strategy at each
SF, we execute 50 paired updates of its terminal relation on the normalized and
de-normalized schemas, with each case reported as the median of ten repetitions.
For each pair, we define the normalization update
speedup as $S_U=U_D/U_N$ and report its median across the 50 cases. We also
measure the one-time cost of normalizing each de-normalized database.

\begin{figure*}[t]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/experiments/update_speedup_by_strategy_nation.png}
    \includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/experiments/update_speedup_by_strategy_region.png}
    \caption{Effect of the TPC-H scale factor on 15 NATION strategies (upper
    pair) and 16 REGION strategies (lower pair). Within each
    pair, median update speedup is shown on the left and one-time normalization
    time on the right.}
    \label{fig:sf_influence}
\end{figure*}

Figure~\ref{fig:sf_influence} shows that increasing SF generally amplifies the
update benefit of normalization for both relations when redundancy grows. For
NATION strategies 9--15, the median speedup rises from $2.22$--$4.33\times$ at
SF = 0.01 to $14.79$--$41.46\times$ at SF = 0.1. For REGION strategies 10--16, the
median speedup rises from $6.76$--$15.98\times$ at SF = 0.01 to
$72.07$--$173.64\times$ at SF = 0.1. REGION strategy 16 illustrates the mechanism:
its additional property cells increase from 1.86M to 18.54M, while
de-normalized update latency rises from 85.1 to 995.4~ms and the normalized
baseline remains near 6~ms. The near-$1\times$ result for REGION strategy 1 (NR)
reflects runtime noise. For REGION, the observed one-time normalization cost also rises
from 0.27--6.00~s to 0.32--65.74~s, showing that greater scale magnifies both
the recurring update advantage and the up-front normalization cost.

\subsection{Limited Query Overhead of Normalization}

To assess the query-performance trade-off between normalized and de-normalized
schemas, we compare each de-normalization strategy with its corresponding
normalized baseline at SF = 0.1. Each pair executes the same parametrized
query instances, and we compare their mean query times. We report only
strategies for which all query executions complete with exact times and the
de-normalized schema is faster. Let $T_D$ and $T_N$ denote the mean query times
of the de-normalized and normalized schemas, respectively. We report
$\Delta_Q=T_N-T_D>0$ together with the time required to construct the
corresponding de-normalized schema.

Across the 74 evaluated strategies,
Table~\ref{tab:denorm_query_advantage} reports 21 exact cases across eight of
the 16 evaluated queries in which de-normalization is faster than the
normalized baseline. Even within this subset, the gain from de-normalization
ranges from 0.4 to 12.3~ms, with a median of 4.9~ms. The largest gain occurs for
Q9 with $\{e_2\}$. This gain is strongly query dependent because among the
queries evaluated using $e_2$ alone, only Q9 benefits from $L\rightarrow O$.
Constructing the corresponding representations takes 0.1 to
96.6~s, a cost that must be amortized over repeated query executions. Overall,
de-normalization improves query performance in only a minority of cases and
incurs build costs that are large relative to its per-query gains.



\section{Graph Embedding Evaluation}


To examine how normalization and de-normalization affect embedding
similarity between child nodes sharing the same parent, we conduct a
paired comparison across nine Northwind child--parent relationships.
For each relationship, the normalized representation retains the child and
parent as separate nodes, whereas the de-normalized representation copies
the parent attributes into each child and inherits the remaining incident relationships.
Child features exclude the foreign key to the selected parent. Parent features retain
all declared fields. We construct pairs of child nodes known to share the same
parent and apply the same embedding strategy to both representations, holding
the evaluated pairs, embedding dimension, feature construction, random seed,
and algorithm configuration constant. We evaluate five embedding methods that
differ in their use of node properties and graph structure.


\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
    \item \textit{Property Hash:} Feature hashing maps node properties to
    vectors without using graph structure.

    \item \textit{FastRP:} Random projection and iterative neighborhood
    aggregation combine node properties with graph structure.

    \item \textit{HashGNN:} Random hash functions aggregate features from
    each node and its neighbors without requiring model training.

    \item \textit{GraphSAGE:} Neighbour sampling and a learned aggregation
    function combine node properties with graph structure.

    \item \textit{Node2Vec:} Random walks provide node contexts for learning
    embeddings from graph structure without node properties.
\end{itemize}

For the overall comparison, the graph-based methods use the full Northwind
graph under the Undirected projection.
Table~\ref{tab:embedding_summary} reports the median cosine similarity
for each method under the normalized and de-normalized representations.
Higher similarity means that child nodes sharing the same parent
are represented more similarly in the embedding space. However, it does not measure
prediction accuracy, because the experiment includes only same-parent pairs and
does not evaluate a downstream classifier. Following this overall comparison,
we use Order--Customer as a focused case study. It contains all 4,941 Order pairs
sharing one of 88 Customers. Using FastRP on the full Northwind graph under
both Natural and Undirected projections, we conduct two parameter sweeps.
First, we vary \texttt{propertyRatio} from 0 to 1
in increments of 0.1, yielding 11 evenly spaced settings, while fixing
\texttt{iterationWeights} to $[0,1,1]$. The parameter specifies the proportion of
embedding dimensions allocated to the property-derived component: 0 allocates all
dimensions to the topology component, whereas 1 allocates all dimensions to the
property component. Second, with \texttt{propertyRatio} fixed at 0.5, we vary the
propagation depth from 1 to 10. For depth $h$, we use an \texttt{iterationWeights}
vector of $h$ unit values, assigning equal weight to each iteration. We retain
the default \texttt{nodeSelfInfluence} of zero in both sweeps. For each pair,
$S_N$ and $S_D$ denote the cosine similarities under the normalized and de-normalized
representations, respectively. We report their medians and the median paired
difference, $\widetilde{\Delta}_S =
\operatorname{median}_i(S_{D,i}-S_{N,i})$, where $i$ indexes the evaluated pairs.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=0.47\textwidth]{figures/experiments/embedding_case.png}
    \caption{FastRP similarity for Order--Customer under Natural and Undirected
    projections, with varying property ratios and hop counts.}
    \label{fig:embedding_case}
\end{figure}

Table~\ref{tab:embedding_summary} shows that de-normalization yields higher
median same parent cosine similarity in 29 of the 45 comparisons. It is higher
in all nine cases for Property Hash. This pattern is
expected because Property Hash uses only node properties: copying the same
parent attributes into each child introduces shared features that tend to
increase the cosine similarity of same-parent pairs. De-normalization also
yields higher medians in five cases each for FastRP and GraphSAGE, seven for
HashGNN, and three for Node2Vec. Order--Customer
illustrates the variation across methods: normalization yields higher medians
for FastRP, Node2Vec, HashGNN, and GraphSAGE, whereas de-normalization is higher
only for Property Hash. The focused FastRP study in
Fig.~\ref{fig:embedding_case} examines how directed versus undirected
projections, the relative emphasis on structural and property information,
and propagation depth affect embedding similarity in normalized and
de-normalized representations. Under the Natural projection, both
representations yield zero similarity scores throughout the property-ratio
sweep. Order nodes point to Customer, Employee, and Shipper before
de-normalization, and to Employee and Shipper afterwards; these neighbors have
no outgoing edges in the projection. The default weights $[0,1,1]$ discard
the only potentially non-zero contribution from the first iteration. With
\texttt{nodeSelfInfluence}=0, the final vectors are zero, which our scoring
function maps to zero similarity. The hop sweep retains
the first-iteration contribution through unit weights, producing median
similarities of 0.491 and 0.209 for the normalized and de-normalized
representations, respectively. Both remain unchanged from one to ten hops
because no directed paths longer than one hop are available from the evaluated
nodes.
Under the Undirected projection, normalization yields higher median
same-parent cosine similarity at every tested property ratio and hop count.
After an initial widening of the gap, increasing \texttt{propertyRatio} from
0.1 to 1.0 brings the median paired difference closer to zero, from $-0.213$
to $-0.043$. Increasing the hop count from 1 to 10 raises the normalized and
de-normalized medians from 0.471 to 0.952 and from 0.377 to 0.914,
respectively. The paired difference initially widens at two hops, then
narrows from $-0.109$ to $-0.038$ at ten hops. Thus, normalization
consistently yields higher same-parent similarity in this case, while
greater property emphasis and propagation beyond two hops bring
de-normalization closer without reversing the ordering.
